questions.q: What does "validate" mean in the triage process Jordan runs against Alert A?
options: Confirming the underlying failed-login events are real and were accurately collected, before judging intent
Immediately disabling the service account as a precaution
Assuming the alert is a false positive because it involves a service account
Waiting for a second analyst to independently confirm the same alert
questions.explain: Validate confirms the events themselves are real and correctly parsed before any judgment about intent happens.

questions.q: Why is Alert A ultimately classified as a false positive rather than a credential-stuffing attempt?
options: A documented password-rotation change ticket explains the failed logins with a known, self-inflicted root cause
Service accounts can never generate real security alerts
The SIEM automatically closes any alert involving a backup job
Nine failed logins is too small a number to ever be suspicious
questions.explain: Scoping the alert against the change calendar found the real cause: a credential-sync gap after a routine password rotation.

questions.q: Why is Alert B still logged as a "true positive," even though nothing malicious happened?
options: The anomaly it detected - a genuinely new-country login - really did occur; it was correctly flagged and then validated as legitimate
Because MFA was not used on that login
Because the SIEM made an error and the alert should have never fired
Because the director's account was later disabled
questions.explain: A true positive just means the detected condition actually happened. Whether it's malicious is a separate question answered by scoping.

questions.q: What specifically makes Alert C escalation-worthy rather than another benign new-location login like Alert B?
options: Impossible travel timing combined with an MFA-skipping legacy login and an active mailbox rule forwarding financial emails externally
The account belongs to an accounts-payable clerk instead of a sales director
The login came from a country farther away than Lisbon
The SIEM assigns escalation status randomly to balance analyst workload
questions.explain: Alert C meets Chapter 5's escalation criteria at once: a confirmed compromise indicator plus financial data actively at risk.

questions.q: Why does Chapter 4's correlation logic matter specifically for Alert C?
options: It ties the login anomaly and the mailbox rule change into one composite high-priority alert instead of two separate, lower-priority ones
It automatically disables the compromised account without analyst review
It only applies to failed login events, never to successful ones
It replaces the need for any human triage process
questions.explain: Without that correlation, the login anomaly and the mailbox change would sit as two unrelated, easier-to-miss alerts.
